body: `V` holds values on a grid laid out as `meshgrid` makes it: `X` varies across the columns and `Y` down the rows. `interp2` gives values at query points `(Xq, Yq)`, by `'linear'` interpolation unless another method is given (`'nearest'`, `'cubic'`, `'spline'`, `'makima'`, `'pchip'`). A row `Xq` with a column `Yq` makes a grid. Points outside the grid give `NaN` unless `extrapval` is given. `interp2(V, k)` refines the grid k times, halving the spacing each time.
syntax: Vq = interp2(X, Y, V, Xq, Yq)
With a method, and a value outside the grid.

examples.title: A coarse surface made smooth

pages.summary: Interpolation on a grid in three or any number of dimensions.
body: `interp3` takes the grid as `meshgrid` lays it out (x across the columns, y down the rows, z the pages); `interpn` takes it as `ndgrid` does (the first coordinate down the rows, the second across, and so on), in any number of dimensions. Query vectors of different sizes make a grid for `interpn`. Methods and `extrapval` as for `interp2`.
syntax: Vq = interp3(X, Y, Z, V, Xq, Yq, Zq)
Vq = interpn(X1, X2, ..., V, Xq1, Xq2, ...)
In any number of dimensions, ndgrid's layout.
With a method, and a value outside.

examples.title: A linear function is reproduced exactly
ndgrid's layout, and a grid of queries

pages.summary: Values at scattered points interpolated onto a grid, or at other points.
body: The points are joined into triangles (Delaunay), and the value at a query point comes from the triangle that holds it: `'linear'` by default, or `'nearest'`, `'natural'`, `'cubic'`, `'v4'` for `griddata`. Query points outside the points' convex hull give `NaN`. `griddatan` does the same in any number of dimensions, a point to each row.
syntax: vq = griddata(x, y, v, xq, yq)
vq = griddata(x, y, v, xq, yq, method)
In n dimensions, points as rows.

examples.title: Scattered samples onto a grid
In three dimensions

pages.summary: An interpolant of values on a grid, evaluated like a function.
body: Made once from the grid and the values, then called as `F(xq)` (or `F(xq1, xq2)`, or `F({xg1, xg2})` for a grid of queries) as often as needed. `Method` is `'linear'` unless given (also `'nearest'`, `'next'`, `'previous'`, `'pchip'`, `'cubic'`, `'spline'`, `'makima'`). Outside the grid it extrapolates by the method it was made with, unless `ExtrapolationMethod` says otherwise (`'none'` gives `NaN`). Both are properties that can be changed on the object; changing `Method` leaves `ExtrapolationMethod` as it was.
syntax: In one dimension; `vq = F(xq)` gives values at query points.
On a grid given by its vectors; `F(xq1, xq2)` at points, `F({xg1, xg2})` on a grid.
F = griddedInterpolant(X1, X2, V, method, extrapolation)
From ndgrid arrays, with a method and extrapolation.

examples.title: Methods, and extrapolation

pages.summary: An interpolant of values at scattered points, evaluated like a function.
body: Made once from points and values (triangulated by Delaunay) and called as `F(xq, yq)`. `Method` is `'linear'` (the default), `'nearest'` or `'natural'` (computed as linear here); outside the convex hull it extrapolates linearly unless `ExtrapolationMethod` is `'nearest'` or `'none'`.
syntax: From points and values; `vq = F(xq, yq)` gives values at query points.
From the points as rows, with a method and extrapolation.

examples.title: A plane through scattered points, and nearest values
Contours from scattered samples
examples.intro: Near the edge of the points the triangles grow long and thin, and linear interpolation there is poor, so the grid stays a little inside.

pages.summary: Piecewise cubic interpolation that keeps the shape of the data.
body: Where `spline` makes the smoothest curve and can overshoot between points, `pchip` (piecewise cubic Hermite) keeps the curve monotone wherever the data are and never overshoots a step; `makima` (modified Akima) lies between them, smooth but with little overshoot. With a third input, the values at `xq`; with two, the piecewise polynomial for `ppval`.

examples.title: A step: spline overshoots, pchip does not

pages.summary: Piecewise polynomials: evaluated, made from their pieces, and taken apart.
body: A piecewise polynomial (pp-form) has breaks `b(1) < b(2) < ...` and, for each piece, the coefficients of a polynomial in `x - b(i)`, highest power first. `spline`, `pchip`, `makima` and `csaps` make them; `mkpp` builds one by hand, `unmkpp` gives back the breaks, coefficients, number of pieces, order and dimension, and `ppval` evaluates.
syntax: From breaks and a row of coefficients for each piece.

examples.title: A spline taken apart
examples.code:
pp = spline(0:3, [0 1 0 1]);
[breaks, coefs, l, k] = unmkpp(pp)

body: The data are taken as one period of a periodic signal: their Fourier coefficients are padded with zeros, and the inverse transform gives `n` points over the same period. For a smooth periodic signal it is exact up to the frequencies the data can hold.

examples.title: Eight samples of a sine, made 32

pages.summary: Smoothing splines: a cubic spline that follows noisy data without going through every point.
body: `csaps(x, y, p)` minimizes `p*sum((y - f(x)).^2) + (1 - p)*integral(f''^2)`: p = 1 interpolates, p = 0 is the least-squares line, and without `p` a value is chosen from the spacing of `x`. `spaps(x, y, tol)` instead asks for the roughest-least spline whose sum of squared errors is at most `tol`. Both return a piecewise polynomial for `fnval`, `ppval` or `fnplt`; with points `xx`, `csaps` gives values.
syntax: With the values at `x` and the weight of the error.

examples.title: Noise smoothed two ways
examples.intro: With noise of standard deviation 0.2 at 60 points, a tolerance of 60*0.2^2 asks the curve to miss by about the noise.

pages.summary: Splines in B-form: interpolating of any order, or made from knots and coefficients.
body: A B-form spline is a sum of B-splines on a knot sequence, each scaled by a coefficient; the order k is the degree plus 1. `spapi(k, x, y)` interpolates the data with a spline of order k; `spmak(knots, coefs)` builds one from its knots and coefficients. Evaluate them with `fnval`, draw them with `fnplt`.

examples.title: A cubic interpolant, and a single B-spline

pages.summary: A spline's values, derivative, integral and parts, and its plot.
body: These work on splines in pp-form (from `spline`, `csaps`, `mkpp`) or B-form (`spmak`, `spapi`), and give results in the same form. `fnder` differentiates (a negative order integrates), `fnint` integrates from the left end of the spline's interval, `fnbrk` gives its parts (`'breaks'`, `'coefs'`, `'pieces'`, `'order'`, `'interval'`, ...), and `fnplt` draws it over its interval.
syntax: The derivative of order `dorder` (1 unless given).
The integral, `value` at the left end (0 unless given).

examples.title: A spline of x^2, its slope and its area
examples.code:
pp = spline(0:4, (0:4).^2);
fnval(pp, 2.5)
fnval(fnder(pp), 2.5)
fnval(fnint(pp), 4)
fnbrk(pp, 'breaks')

examples.title: A spline and its derivative drawn
examples.code:
pp = spline(0:6, [0 1 0 -1 0 1 0]);
fnplt(pp), hold on
fnplt(fnder(pp), 'r--'), hold off
grid on, legend('spline', 'derivative')
